title: Checkpoint: Samples and Polls
objective: After this level you can judge whether a poll or survey can be trusted from how its sample was drawn and its questions asked.
summary: Judge a poll by its label: was the sample random or opt-in, who answered, how it was weighted, its size and margin, and how the questions were worded.

cards.headline: A poll lands in your feed. Before you share it, read the label.
cards.body: Good pollsters publish how a poll was made, a bit like an ingredients list. Chapter 6 has taught you what each ingredient means. This checkpoint puts them together.

cards.headline: What honest pollsters disclose
cards.body: AAPOR, the survey researchers' professional association, asks pollsters to disclose who paid for the poll, the exact question wording, the population studied, whether the sample was random or opt-in, the sample size and margin of error, how answers were weighted, and when it was done. Pew notes that pollsters who explain their methods clearly and in detail tend to be more accurate.

items.label: Who was picked?
points: Random: everyone had the same chance

items.label: Who answered?
points: Nonresponse skews when the topic drives it
Weighting fixes the mix, not everything

items.label: How sure, how asked?
points: Wording can move answers outside the margin

cards.headline: One pot, one last time
cards.body: Every check comes back to Level 51's soup. Was the pot stirred, so every spoonful had the same chance? Did the spoon reach the whole pot, or only the people keen to answer? Is the spoon big enough to trust, give or take the margin? And did you ask "How's the soup?" or "Isn't this soup too salty?"

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Why a random sample of about 1,000 people can speak for a whole country.
How the 1936 Literary Digest got 2.4 million answers and still picked the wrong winner.
What a margin of error covers, and why a lead needs about double the margin.
How nonresponse, weighting, wording and opt-in clicks can each bend a poll.

questions.prompt: Which of these do AAPOR's standards ask pollsters to disclose?

options.label: The names of everyone interviewed
options.rationale: Respondents stay anonymous; methods are disclosed.

options.label: The answer the sponsor hoped for
options.rationale: The sponsor is named, not its hopes.

options.label: The exact wording of the questions
The pollster's own opinion on the topic
options.rationale: Disclosure is about methods, not opinions.

questions.explanation: AAPOR asks for the sponsor, exact wording, population, random or opt-in sample, size and margin, weighting and dates.

questions.prompt: Why can a random sample of 1,000 beat 2.4 million replies drawn from phone and car lists?

options.label: Smaller polls are always more accurate
options.rationale: Size isn't the reason; bigger random samples are more precise.

options.label: Randomness removes bias, and size only shrinks chance error
Older polls counted ballots by hand
A thousand is the legal minimum for polls

questions.explanation: A tilted sample stays tilted however large. Random selection gives everyone the same chance; size then adds precision.

questions.prompt: A poll shows candidate A at 47% and B at 44%, each ±3. What's the fair headline?

options.label: A leads by a clear 3 points
options.rationale: The margin on the lead is about 6 points.

options.label: Too close to call: the lead is under about 6 points
B is certain to lose
options.rationale: A 3-point lead is well within the margin on the gap.

options.label: A leads by 3 percent
options.rationale: The gap is 3 percentage points, and it's within the margin.

questions.explanation: With ±3 on each share, the margin on the gap is about 6 points. A 3-point lead is too close to call.

questions.prompt: A poll reached too few young adults. What's the usual fix, and its limit?

options.label: Delete older people's answers until balanced
options.rationale: Pollsters weight answers rather than throw them away.

options.label: Report it as an opt-in poll
options.rationale: It's still a random sample; it just needs weighting.

options.label: Double the margin of error and publish
options.rationale: The fix is weighting, which widens the margin somewhat.

options.label: Count their answers more; it can't fix biases it doesn't measure

questions.explanation: Weighting counts underrepresented groups more so the mix matches, but it only balances the traits it weights on.

questions.prompt: Match each poll check with what it means.
questions.explanation: In a random sample everyone had the same chance; in an opt-in poll people picked themselves. Weighting fixes the mix, not everything, and about 1,000 random people give about ±3 points.
